newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin keeps low profile, foes step up attacks.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin keeps low profile, foes step up attacks.

text.p: Russian President Yeltsin, recovering from pneumonia in a country residence, kept a low profile on Tuesday while his political foes in parliament unveiled plans to force him from office on health grounds.

A Kremlin spokesman said Yeltsin, who left the elite Central Clinical Hospital on Monday after nearly two weeks of treatment, was convalescing in the Gorky-9 residence outside Moscow and did not plan any official meetings.
The president was ill with heart problems for most of the second half of last year, and this and the pneumonia raised doubts about his ability to complete his second term in office.

The Kremlin says Yeltsin's pneumonia is not linked to his heart operation. U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, who advised the president before and during the operation, has said it should give him 10 more years of active work.
Yeltsin aides expect the president to be fit for a summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States and to hold talks with visiting French President Jaques Chirac in the next two weeks.
But Yeltsin's opponents remain unimpressed and insist that the president should step down.
The council of the State Duma lower house of parliament said the chamber would debate on Wednesday a controversial draft which would remove Yeltsin from office for health reasons.
Duma legal experts have said a parliamentary declaration was insufficient to launch impeachment procedings against Yeltsin. They described the draft as unconstitutional and invalid.
The constitution does not outline a mechanism under which a president can be ousted on health grounds and the Kremlin has said a parliamentary decision would have no legal force.
But approval of the draft or a prolonged Yeltsin absence could prompt a fresh bout of political infighting.

As a first shot in this tug-of-war, the opposition-dominated Duma agreed on Tuesday to debate a new request to the president to investigate his chief aide, Anatoly Chubais, in connection with allegations of financial irregularities.

Communist Viktor Ilyukhin, head of the Duma's influential security committee, told reporters he had drafted a motion alleging that Chubais might have broken laws barring officials from earning money privately. A debate is likely on Friday.

Chubais was one of the architects of Yeltsin's free market reforms and privatisations and he is a prime target for the communists. He was not immediately available for comment, but he has strenuously denied previous accusations of financial irregularities.
Ilyukhin distributed photocopies of what purported to be a credit card statement for an account belonging to Chubais.

Ilyukhin said they corroborated allegations that Chubais received significant dollar payments whhile he was running Yeltsin's re-election campaign and after he was appointed to run the Kremlin administration in July.
